name: Yara Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Yara, I'm 27, and I'm a reporter for a group of three weekly papers covering a market town and the villages around it. I do school sports, village shows, golden weddings and the tributes when someone local dies. I live with my partner Owen, who's an electrician, in a small rented house off the high street.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Monday and Tuesday I'm on the phone and out with my camera at fixtures and fêtes, Wednesday is deadline, and Thursday the papers come out and I start again. I like the tributes more than you'd think, because families tell you things about a person nobody ever wrote down. I'm slow, though, and Dawn, the group editor, often has to cut my pieces in half. What wears me out is the drive, because they shut our town office and now I'm based in a unit forty minutes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, then, and get on with it. I don't do the online arguments, so I'd just mention it in the office. Probably something like: well, that's one less thing to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't change much for me, because the papers were struggling anyway. The group's been sold twice since I started, and every time there are fewer of us. Adverts from estate agents and car dealers were what paid my wage, and they've mostly moved online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and try to write tighter, so Dawn isn't cutting me every week. I'd keep putting a bit by each month, because we've got about two months of savings. And I'd keep an eye on the jobs board at the council, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, really. A world without clever AI still has a weekly paper that loses another advertiser every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the group's been sold twice. What happened each time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First time they closed the town office and moved us to the industrial estate. Second time they stopped paying for a photographer, so now I take my own pictures on a work phone. Each owner promises it's the last change, and it never is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a bill you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fuel, honestly, because I drive everywhere for fixtures and the mileage allowance doesn't cover it. Owen's work is steady, so rent's fine. But I hate not pulling my weight.

say: I'd say **fair enough** and get on with the job.
I'd mention it in the office as **one less thing** to worry about.
think: I think the papers were **struggling anyway**, AI or not.
Lost **estate agent** and car adverts were what paid my wage.
do: Write **tighter** so the editor stops cutting my pieces.
Watch the **council jobs board** just in case.
S0.quote: A world without clever AI still has a weekly paper that loses another advertiser every month.
fieldNote: Yara's pressure comes from **falling adverts** and two changes of owner, not from AI.
She's **practical and quiet**, avoids online debate and talks in plain terms.
Partner Owen's **steady trade** covers the rent, which she feels guilty about.

steps.text: Write shorter, tighter match reports each week
Put a set amount into savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sad, and that people will miss the paper when it's gone. I'd say it to readers at fixtures, because they ask me if we're closing. I wouldn't make a fuss online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the group would use it to get rid of the slow ones, and I'm one of the slow ones. Results, wedding write-ups, the what's-on column, that's all writing from things people send in, and a computer could do it from the forms. I don't use the AI stuff at all, so I wouldn't even look useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start applying for jobs that are steadier, like the council's communications team or a school office, within the first few months. I'd stop the subscriptions and drive less, maybe ask to cover fixtures by phone. And I'd talk to Owen about how long we could manage on his wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried sick, but trying not to show it. I'd go quiet, which Owen says is how he knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a computer could do the write-ups from the forms. Is there anything it couldn't do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tributes, maybe. Families tell me things at the kitchen table about their mum that they'd never type into a form for a computer. But the group doesn't pay me for the tributes, it pays me to fill pages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not try the AI tools, if it would make you look useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be bad at them, and slow, and I'd be learning them just to train my own replacement. That's how it feels, anyway. Maybe I'm wrong, but I'd rather put my time into getting out.

say: I'd say readers will **miss the paper** when it's gone.
I'd keep it to people at **fixtures**, not online.
think: I think the group would cut **the slow ones**, including me.
Write-ups from **forms people send** are easy for a computer.
do: Apply to the **council communications** team or a school office.
Work out how long we'd last on **Owen's wage**.
feel: **Worried sick**, but going quiet instead of showing it.
S1.quote: Families tell me things at the kitchen table about their mum that they'd never type into a form for a computer.
fieldNote: Yara expects to be cut and won't learn AI, seeing it as **training her replacement**.
She values the **tributes** most, but knows the group pays for filled pages.
Her plan is to **leave first**, toward steady local jobs.

steps.text: Apply for council communications or school office jobs
Cancel streaming subscriptions and cut driving
Lean on Owen's electrician wage while job-hunting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happened too fast and someone should have seen it coming. I'd probably say that to my mum on the phone and to Owen, and not much further. I'm not one for marches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd assume the papers are finished inside a year. My whole job is writing and phoning, so it's the thinking work that goes first. Owen's job is hands-on, so he'd have till about 2031, and that would be our lifeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask Owen whether I could do the bookings and invoices for his work, and help on site, to keep money in the house. I'd cut everything we don't need: takeaways, my gym, the holiday fund. And I'd talk to my parents about whether we could move in with them for a while if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and stuck. Like the floor's gone and I'm waiting to land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Owen's bookings and invoices are thinking work too. Wouldn't AI do those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You're right, it would, and I hadn't thought of that. Then I'd be carrying cable and sweeping up, I suppose. I'd rather sweep up after my partner Owen on a building site than sit at home waiting for the paper to call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving in with your parents mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Back to my old room at 28, in the village I couldn't wait to leave. Mum would love it, Dad would make jokes. But it would mean we'd have Owen's wage and no rent for a year, which is a lot of breathing room.

say: I'd say it came **too fast** and someone should have seen it.
I'd keep it to **family**; I'm not one for marches.
think: I think the papers are **finished inside a year**, because my job is all writing and phoning.
Owen's **hands-on** job gives us until about 2031.
do: Help on **Owen's jobs** with site work and paperwork.
Cut **takeaways**, the gym and the holiday fund.
Ask my parents about **moving in** for a year.
S2.quote: I'd rather sweep up after my partner Owen on a building site than sit at home waiting for the paper to call.
fieldNote: Yara sees the **robot gap** clearly through Owen's trade, which becomes the household lifeline.
She hadn't realised **admin work** is also exposed and accepts it when it's pointed out.
**Moving home** is a real option she'd take, despite her pride.

steps.text: Work alongside Owen on electrical jobs, doing site help
Stop takeaways, the gym and the holiday fund
Ask her parents for help with money and housing
Move into her parents' house for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, so let's get ready. I'd say it to the other reporters, the ones who'll listen. Not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd leave the paper within a couple of years, while I still choose when. I'd be 32 by 2031, which is young enough to train. Owen's trade lasts a bit longer, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look at becoming a teaching assistant, because I already know half the PE teachers from fixtures. I'd stay at the paper while I do the course in the evenings. And I'd save harder, aiming for four months instead of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I could see a path. That makes a difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a teaching assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm at the schools every week anyway, and the kids are the best part of the job. A machine can write up the under-11s netball score, but it can't stand on the sideline and calm a crying nine-year-old. I'd be good at that bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it cost you to make the switch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pay cut, probably, which hurts. Teaching assistants don't earn much, less than me. But it's a job that's there in every village, and I wouldn't be driving forty minutes each way.

say: I'd say there's **time to get ready**, so we should start now.
I'd tell the **other reporters** who'll listen, not post online.
think: I think I'd leave the paper **within two years** on my terms.
At **32** I'd still be young enough to train.
do: Train as a **teaching assistant** in the evenings.
Stay at the paper while I **study**.
Raise savings from two to **four months**.
S3.quote: A machine can write up the under-11s netball score, but it can't stand on the sideline and calm a crying nine-year-old.
fieldNote: Five years lets Yara pick a **familiar** route: schools she already visits weekly.
She accepts a **pay cut** for work that's local and in person.
Her fear eases from alarmed because she has **time and a plan**.

steps.text: Take an evening course to become a teaching assistant
Raise savings from two to four months of costs
Apply for teaching assistant jobs at local primary schools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the paper might not last that long anyway. I'd say it at the pub quiz when it came up. That's about as far as I'd take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably just carry on for now. Ten years feels too far off to do anything drastic. I'd be 37, which is a different person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the paper, keep trying to write tighter, and keep saving. I'd look at the teaching assistant idea in a few years if the paper was still going downhill. I'd wait and see what the first couple of years looked like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but the paper still worries me. It's the paper, not the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would make you stop waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Another sale of the group, or the papers going online only. Either one and I'd start the course that month. The weekly paper has been sold twice already, and a third sale would get me out faster than any AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want to be doing at 37?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where I'm not in the car all day. Maybe at a school. Maybe still writing tributes for families, if anyone still wants them done by a person.

say: I'd say ten years is long, and the **paper may not last**.
I'd mention it at the **pub quiz**, not further.
think: I think I'd **carry on** at the paper for now.
Ten years feels **too far off** for drastic steps, since I'd be a different person at 37.
do: Stay at the paper and **write tighter**.
Revisit the **teaching assistant** course in a few years.
S4.quote: The weekly paper has been sold twice already, and a third sale would get me out faster than any AI.
fieldNote: With ten years Yara **waits and sees**, true to her resistant streak.
Her trigger to act is a **third sale** of the group, not AI.
Her anxiety stays because the **paper's decline** is already under way.

steps.text: Keep covering school sports and tributes at the paper
Keep saving a set amount each month
Wait for the group's next sale before deciding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be out of work before I'd even worked out what else I could do. What would help is a cheap, local course into school jobs, and help with fuel or travel while I retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people would lose. When the weekly paper goes, nobody writes down that a woman ran the village shop for forty years. That bothers me more than my own job, some days.

headlineQuote: When the weekly paper goes, nobody writes down that a woman ran the village shop for forty years.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old** reporter on three weekly papers, covering school sports, shows and tributes.
She's **slow and self-critical**, never uses AI, and keeps her views off social media.
The paper's **falling adverts** worry her even in the mildest picture.
Partner Owen's **electrician work** is the household's lifeline when AGI arrives.
With time she'd become a **teaching assistant**, trading pay for local, in-person work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd lose work before she had any plan.
whatWouldHelp: A cheap, **local course** into school jobs and help with **travel costs** while retraining.
